comments.text: The Constraints section records "privacy" as considered and not applying, but the register holds personal data about real people (names and ages) and is explicitly intended as "the reference list other features can point at" — i.e. its rows will be read across the business. It would be worth either stating a constraint here (e.g. retention, or that the data is limited to name and age by design, which the Scope OUT list already implies) or a one-clause reason why the platform's default handling suffices, so a later reviewer doesn't mistake the bare "none apply" for an oversight.

Addressed in the Constraints section: the register now states that it holds personal data by design — a name and an age, and nothing else — with retention and access following the platform's default handling, flagged as an assumption for the author to confirm if a retention rule applies.

text: A register of persons — the people the business deals with — holding each person's name and age. It gives any signed-in user a place to create, browse, edit and retire person records, and serves as the reference list other features can point at.

text: No uniqueness rule was requested — two persons may share a name and an age.

comments.text: Clarification for reviewers: this is a decision, not an omission. Two different people can legitimately be called the same name and be the same age, so Person has no unique key beyond its system id. If the business later wants 'same name + same age = same person' detection, that is a new rule to spec, not a bug here.

text: | status | lifecycle(draft, active, retired) | yes | default(draft) |

comments.text: Clarification on the lifecycle: draft = newly keyed in, not yet in use; active = in use as a reference by other features; retired = no longer selectable for new business but kept for history. Note the status field was added by the agent as standard bean practice — the original request named only name and age — so drop it from the table if the register should hold no lifecycle at all.
